newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany takes aim at big Eurocrat salaries.
newsitem.headline: Germany takes aim at big Eurocrat salaries.

text.p: Bloated salaries enjoyed by European Union bureaucrats could be a thing of the past if Germany gets its way in the EU's current round of treaty negotiations.

Werner Hoyer, Germany's secretary of state for Europe, said on Tuesday that Bonn wanted to rein in growth of pay and benefits of EU officials by handing responsibility for salary increases to member states rather than the European Commission.

"We can no longer ignore the pressure of public opinion on this issue," he told reporters, adding that with Germany, 12 of the 15 EU countries had signalled support for the move during discussions on a new EU treaty.

Hoyer said the move was not just a matter of courting popular support. High salaries among Eurocrats were tarnishing the EU's image in Europe at a time of sharp budget discipline to meet the goals of economic and monetary union.
Pressure to act is strong in Germany where an auditors court has criticised the generous pay of EU officials and asked Bonn to do something about it.
Newspapers in the EU's Nordic countries have also been regaling their readers with tales of the delights of Brussels, where a middle-ranking bureaucrat can be paid more than a Finnish prime minister.
Hoyer cited as an example the European patent office, located in Munich a few hundred metres (yards) from its German equivalent.
The European salaries at the office are twice as high as those of their German neighbours.
In Brussels, where most of the roughly 30,000 EU officials work for various EU institutions, a secretary earns three times that of a Belgian counterpart.
Salaries for the most senior officials, however, are nearer to those of member state officials of equal rank.
Hoyer said he wanted the EU treaty to be amended to let the Council of Ministers, the body made up of member states, recommend salary increases.
Rises are currently recommended by the European Commission, based on a system that was set up years ago before the corps of EU officials expanded.
The Commission has tried to change the system in the past, but was immediately subject to a strike by some 20,000 workers.
"If the Commission cannot resolve the problem, the Council of Ministers must," Hoyer said.
